adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The town of Bellweather sits at the end of a narrow road that follows the salt marsh for nearly six miles before it reaches the water. In winter the population falls below four hundred, and the only shop that stays open is the hardware store beside the old grist mill. For most of the twentieth century the harbour supported a modest fleet of lobster boats, but the catch has declined for thirty years and the younger families have moved inland, where the rents are lower and the work is steadier. The school closed in 1998; the children are bused to the regional school forty minutes away.

Last spring the select board appointed a committee to study the future of the waterfront. The committee met on Tuesday evenings in the basement of the library, around a folding table borrowed from the fire hall. Its members were a retired teacher, two fishermen, a carpenter, the owner of the hardware store, and a woman named Edith Harmon, who had run the summer theatre for two decades and who, everyone agreed, knew how to keep a meeting moving.

The first weeks were spent on arithmetic. The committee counted moorings, measured the length of the seawall, and listed every building within the flood plain. They argued about the cost of dredging and about whether the state would pay for any of it. They argued about parking, about the smell of the bait house in August, and about whether the ice cream stand should be allowed to stay open past nine.

By June the arguments had settled into a familiar pattern. The fishermen wanted the pier repaired and the channel cleared. The carpenter wanted the old boathouse converted into a workshop. The teacher wanted a small museum in the net shed, with photographs of the fleet as it had been in the fifties. The owner of the hardware store wanted nothing at all, and said so at every meeting, usually while looking at his watch.

Edith Harmon rarely spoke during these exchanges. She took notes in a spiral notebook, and when the talk began to circle she would read back what had been said, in order, until the room grew quiet. The others came to rely on this without ever saying so.

In July the state historic commission sent a letter. It proposed to nominate the entire waterfront as a district, which would bring money for restoration but also restrictions on what owners could do to their buildings. The letter arrived on a Friday and was read aloud the following Tuesday. The reaction was immediate and loud. The carpenter said the commission had no business telling him how to repair his own roof. One of the fishermen said the district would bring tourists, and that tourists were the only crop the town had left. Another said the commission would find a way to charge for parking.

The chair let the argument run for almost an hour. Then, when the room had exhausted itself, she spoke of the harbour fund that had been quietly accumulating interest since the eighties, money that no one had ever agreed how to spend. She regarded the silence that followed as a reproach rather than consent, and she said so, plainly, before asking for a vote.
